questions.question: Describe the four-sector circular flow: name the participants and their functions, the four markets where they meet, and the two flows that run around the diagram.
questions.expected_answer: The four participants are households, businesses, government and the foreign sector; including the foreign sector is what makes the model open rather than closed. Households own and supply the factors of production and receive wages, rent, interest and profit, which they consume, save and pay tax on. Businesses hire factor services, produce goods and services, pay out incomes and invest in capital goods. Government taxes, spends on goods, services and transfers, and provides public goods; the foreign sector buys exports and supplies imports. They meet in the factor market, the product market, the financial market and the foreign exchange market. Two flows run in opposite directions: the real flow of factor services and goods, and the money flow of incomes and expenditure facing it — every real movement has a money movement opposite it, which is why the diagram closes.

questions.question: State the equilibrium condition for an open economy, test it with S = 250, T = 550, M = 300, I = 300, G = 500, X = 300 (R billions), and trace what happens when exports then fall to 240.
questions.expected_answer: Equilibrium requires total leakages to equal total injections: S + T + M = I + G + X. Leakages are 250 + 550 + 300 = R1 100 billion and injections are 300 + 500 + 300 = R1 100 billion, so the economy is in equilibrium — noting that individual pairs need not match (T exceeds G by 50 while I exceeds S by 50); only the totals must agree. If exports fall to 240, injections drop to R1 040 billion against leakages of R1 100 billion. Stock accumulates, firms cut production and retrench, incomes fall, and because incomes are lower, households save less, pay less tax and import less, so the leakages shrink. Equilibrium is restored at a lower level of national income with higher unemployment — a downswing told in circular-flow terms.

questions.question: Explain the three methods of measuring the flow, then convert GDP at market prices of R7 000 billion into GDP at factor cost and into GNI, given taxes on products of R800 billion, subsidies on products of R120 billion, primary income received from abroad of R90 billion and primary income paid abroad of R260 billion, and finally deflate the nominal figure with a deflator of 125.
questions.expected_answer: The flow is measured at three points that must agree: the production method sums value added by every producer (value added, not turnover, so intermediate goods are not double-counted); the income method sums compensation of employees, net operating surplus and consumption of fixed capital; the expenditure method sums C + I + G + (X − M). GDP at factor cost = market prices − taxes on products + subsidies on products = 7 000 − 800 + 120 = R6 320 billion. GNI = GDP + primary income received from abroad − primary income paid abroad = 7 000 + 90 − 260 = R6 830 billion; because more foreign-owned capital operates in South Africa than South African capital abroad, GNI sits structurally below GDP. Real GDP = 7 000 × 100 ÷ 125 = R5 600 billion; spread over roughly 63 million people this is about R89 000 per person, and if real GDP grows more slowly than the population, output per person falls even while the economy nominally grows.
